summary: A best current practice that says specifications of protocols using transient numeric identifiers must consider the security and privacy consequences of how they are generated. Poor choices have caused attacks like denial of service, data injection, and information leaks.

plainLanguage.summary: Many protocols pick a fresh number each time they act: a TCP sequence number, a port number, a DNS query ID. If an attacker can work out the next number, the attacker can inject packets, break connections or follow what a device is doing. This Best Current Practice says a protocol specification must state what its numbers have to achieve, must assess the risk of how they are produced, and must not ask for predictable values.

subtitle: What protocol specifications must say about numbers they pick at random, such as sequence numbers and port numbers.

tldr.problem: Poorly chosen transient numeric identifiers, such as TCP sequence numbers, IPv6 interface identifiers and DNS IDs, have enabled denial of service, data injection and information leaks for more than 30 years.
tldr.mechanism: Specifications that use such identifiers MUST state their interoperability requirements and the severity of failing them, MUST include a vulnerability assessment, SHOULD avoid predictable values, and SHOULD recommend a generation algorithm that mitigates the findings.
tldr.outcome: The RFC formally updates RFC 3552, so the security and privacy effects of these identifiers are covered in the Security Considerations section of future RFCs.

facts.label: Threat classes the assessment must cover
facts.value: Spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege

today: RFC 9416 is a Best Current Practice, BCP 72, published in July 2023. It updates RFC 3552 so that the security and privacy effects of transient numeric identifiers are covered in the Security Considerations section of future RFCs, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Transient Identifiers Need Care
sections.content:
Networking protocols use transient numeric identifiers for many kinds of protocol object: IPv4 and IPv6 Identification values, IPv6 Interface Identifiers (IIDs), transport-protocol ephemeral port numbers, TCP Initial Sequence Numbers (ISNs), NTP Reference IDs (REFIDs) and DNS IDs. These identifiers usually have specific requirements, such as uniqueness during a stated period, that must be satisfied so that they do not cause interoperability problems, together with an associated failure severity when the requirements are not met. Some documents refer to the DNS ID as the DNS Query ID or TxID.

For more than 30 years, a large number of implementations of IETF protocols have been subject to a variety of attacks, with effects ranging from Denial of Service or data injection to information leakages that could be exploited for pervasive monitoring. The root cause of these issues has been, in many cases, the poor selection of transient numeric identifiers, usually as a result of insufficient or misleading specifications. While it is generally trivial to find an algorithm that satisfies the interoperability requirements of a given identifier, empirical evidence exists that doing so without harming the security and privacy properties of the protocols is prone to error.

The document lists the resulting problems: predictable IPv4 or IPv6 Identification values, predictable IPv6 IIDs, predictable transport-protocol ephemeral port numbers, predictable TCP Initial Sequence Numbers, predictable initial timestamps in TCP timestamp options, and predictable DNS IDs.

Recent history indicates that when new protocols are standardized or new implementations are produced, the security and privacy properties of the associated identifiers tend to be overlooked, and inappropriate algorithms to generate them are either suggested in the specifications or selected by implementers. Advice in this area is therefore warranted.

Cryptographic techniques for confidentiality and authentication might not eliminate all the issues, so due diligence is required even when cryptography is employed. Cryptographic authentication can readily mitigate data injection attacks even with predictable identifiers such as sequence numbers. But a flawed algorithm, such as a global counter, could still leak information even when cryptographic techniques are employed, and those leakages could in turn be used for other attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocols pick numbers to identify things that change over time, such as connections and queries. When the next number can be predicted, an attacker can pretend to be the other party. The document says specifications must treat this as a design requirement, not an afterthought.

sections.title: What the Document Calls Things
sections.content:
A transient numeric identifier is a data object in a protocol specification that can be used to definitely distinguish a protocol object, such as a datagram, network interface, transport-protocol endpoint or session, from all other objects of the same type in a given context. These identifiers are usually defined as a series of bits and represented using integer values. They are typically dynamically selected, as opposed to statically assigned numeric identifiers. Different transient numeric identifiers may have additional requirements depending on their specific use in a protocol. The document uses the term as a generic term for any data object in a protocol specification that satisfies the identification property stated above.

A failure severity is the interoperability consequence of failing to comply with the interoperability requirements of a given identifier. Severity considers the worst potential consequence of a failure, determined by the system damage or the time lost to repair it. Two types are defined.

  • A soft failure is a recoverable condition in which a protocol does not operate in the prescribed manner, but normal operation can be resumed automatically in a short period of time. A simple packet-loss event that is recovered with a retransmission is an example.
  • A hard failure is a non-recoverable condition in which a protocol does not operate in the prescribed manner, or operates with excessive degradation of service. An established TCP connection aborted because of an error condition is an example, since from the point of view of the transport protocol it enters a state from which normal operation cannot be recovered.
sections.plainLanguage: The document uses one term for any number a protocol picks to tell objects apart, and it sorts the consequences of getting it wrong into two kinds: recoverable, and not recoverable.

sections.title: Three Ways Specifications Go Wrong
sections.content:
Recent work on transient numeric identifier usage in protocol specifications and implementations revealed that most of the issues in this document arise from one of three conditions: protocol specifications that under specify their transient numeric identifiers, protocol specifications that over specify their transient numeric identifiers, and protocol implementations that simply fail to comply with the specified requirements.

Both under specifying and over specifying is hazardous. TCP local ports and DNS IDs were originally under specified, leading to implementations that produced predictable values and so were vulnerable to numerous off-path attacks. Over specification, as for IPv6 Interface Identifiers and IPv6 Identification values, left implementations unable to respond to security and privacy issues stemming from the mandated or recommended algorithms: IPv6 IIDs need not expose privacy-sensitive link-layer addresses, and predictable IPv6 Fragment Header Identification values invite the same off-path attacks that plague TCP.

Finally, there are implementations that simply fail to comply with existing specifications. Appropriate guidance is provided by the protocol specification, whether the core specification or an update to it, but the implementation does not follow it. Some popular operating systems still fail to implement transport-protocol port randomization, as specified in RFC 6056.

A clear specification of the interoperability requirements will help identify algorithms that could be used to generate the identifiers and will also make evident if the identifiers are being over specified. A protocol specification will usually also benefit from a vulnerability assessment of the transient numeric identifiers it specifies, to prevent the corresponding considerations from being overlooked.
sections.plainLanguage: Specifications fail in three ways: they say too little about the number, they say too much and lock implementations into a bad algorithm, or they say the right thing and the implementation ignores it. Each of the three has caused real attacks.

sections.title: Six Ways to Generate a Bad Identifier
sections.content:
The document lists common flaws in the generation of transient numeric identifiers:

  • Employing trivial algorithms, such as global counters, that result in predictable identifiers. Any node that is able to sample such identifiers can easily predict future identifiers employed by the victim node.
  • Employing the same identifier across contexts in which constancy is not required. This makes activity correlation possible; an identifier that is constant across networks, for example, allows node tracking across networks.
  • Reusing identifiers across different protocols or layers of the protocol stack. This ties the security and privacy properties of the protocol reusing the identifier to those of the original identifier, over which the reusing protocol may have no control regarding its generation. It also breaks the goal of isolating the properties of a layer from those of another layer, and the vulnerability assessment becomes harder to perform because the combined system has to be assessed rather than each protocol in isolation.
  • Initializing counters or timers to constant values when such initialization is not required. At times a protocol needs to convey order information, whether sequence or timing, and in many cases there is no reason for the corresponding counter or timer to be initialized to any specific value, for example at system bootstrap. There may also be no need for the difference between successive counter values to be predictable.
  • Employing the same increment space across different contexts. A node that implements a per-context linear function may share the increment space among different contexts. Sharing the same increment space allows an attacker who can sample identifiers in another context to learn how many identifiers have been generated between two sampled values.
  • Use of flawed Pseudorandom Number Generators. Some implementations have been found to employ flawed PRNGs.
sections.plainLanguage: Most weak identifiers come from a short list of choices: a plain counter, the same value everywhere, a value borrowed from another layer, a fixed starting point, a counter shared between different jobs, or a broken random number generator. Each one gives an attacker something to work with.

sections.title: What a Specification Must Do
sections.content:
Protocol specifications that employ transient numeric identifiers MUST explicitly specify the interoperability requirements for those identifiers, for example required properties such as uniqueness, along with the failure severity if such requirements are not met.

A vulnerability assessment of the identifiers MUST be performed as part of the specification process. Such a vulnerability assessment should cover, at least, spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, Denial of Service, and elevation of privilege.

Protocol specifications SHOULD NOT employ predictable transient numeric identifiers, except when such predictability is the result of their interoperability requirements.

Protocol specifications that employ transient numeric identifiers SHOULD recommend an algorithm for generating them that mitigates the vulnerabilities identified in the previous step, such as those discussed in RFC 9415.

Because the use of cryptographic techniques for confidentiality and authentication might not eliminate all the issues associated with predictable identifiers, the advice in this section MUST still be applied in cases where cryptographic techniques for confidentiality or authentication are employed.
sections.plainLanguage: The specification has to say what the number must guarantee, has to run a security review of it, has to avoid predictable values unless the protocol forces them, and has to recommend an algorithm that avoids the problems found in the review.

sections.title: Security Considerations and the RFC 3552 Update
sections.content:
The document states that the whole of it is about the security and privacy implications of transient numeric identifiers, and it formally updates RFC 3552 so that the security and privacy implications of transient numeric identifiers are addressed when writing the Security Considerations section of future RFCs.

The document has no IANA actions, since it only states requirements for protocol specifications and updates an existing one.
sections.plainLanguage: The document changes how future specifications are written: the section about security has to cover the numbers the protocol picks. It also registers nothing new, because it only sets requirements and updates an existing document.

items.label: Interface Identifier
items.desc: The part of an IPv6 address that identifies one interface.

items.label: Ephemeral port number
items.desc: The port a transport-protocol endpoint picks for one session.

items.label: Initial Sequence Number
items.desc: The first sequence number of a connection.

items.label: Reference ID
items.desc: The identifier used to match a reply to its request.

items.label: Query ID
items.desc: The identifier that matches a DNS reply to its query.

viz.caption: SIX FLAWS IN THE GENERATION OF IDENTIFIERS

items.title: Trivial algorithm
items.text: A global counter, so future values can be predicted.

items.title: Same value across contexts
items.text: Constant everywhere, which allows tracking a node across networks.

items.title: Reused from another layer
items.text: Ties one protocol's security to a value it does not control.

items.title: Fixed starting point
items.text: A counter or timer initialized to a constant value.

items.title: Shared increment space
items.text: Lets an observer count how many values were generated.

items.title: Flawed PRNG
items.text: A pseudorandom generator that can be predicted.
